Magicians
muh-JISH-unz
n. pl.
From Latin magus, through Greek, from the Persian priestly caste. Webster 1828: one skilled in magic; one who practises the black art. In the Authorized Version the magicians are court officials of Egypt and Babylon — professional interpreters and enchanters — and Scripture records exactly where their power stopped.

Biblical Definition

The magicians in Scripture are a professional class attached to a throne, and their story is a story of a limit. In Egypt they fail Pharaoh from the beginning: I told this unto the magicians; but there was none that could declare it to me (Genesis 41:24). At the exodus they keep pace for a time: they turn rods to serpents, water to blood, and bring up frogs with their enchantments (Exodus 7:11, 22; 8:7). Then comes the third plague and the sentence that ends their career: the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not (Exodus 8:18), and they say to Pharaoh, This is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19). Two plagues later they cannot even stand: the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians (Exodus 9:11). In Babylon the pattern repeats. Daniel and his companions are examined and found ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm (Daniel 1:20), and in the next chapter the magicians cannot tell the king his dream. Whatever power they had was real enough to deceive and never enough to save.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MAGICIAN as one skilled in magic; one that practises the black art; an enchanter; a necromancer. In Scripture the term names a recognized office in the courts of Egypt and Babylon.

expand to see more

MAGICIAN, n. — One skilled in magic; one that practises the black art; an enchanter; a necromancer; a sorcerer or sorceress.

MAGIC, n. — The art or science of putting into action the power of spirits; or the science of producing wonderful effects by the aid of superhuman beings.

Webster does not treat magic as empty conjuring, and neither does Scripture. The Egyptian enchanters produced something; the question the narrative presses is not whether they had power but whose power it was and where it ran out.

Key Scripture

Genesis 41:24 — "And the thin ears devoured the seven good ears: and I told this unto the magicians; but there was none that could declare it to me."

Exodus 7:11 — "Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments."

Exodus 8:18 — "And the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not: so there were lice upon man, and upon beast."

Exodus 8:19 — "Then the magicians said unto Pharaoh, This is the finger of God: and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had said."

Daniel 1:20 — "And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm."

Modern Corruption

The magicians are corrupted in modern reading in opposite directions: reduced to stage conjurors whose tricks Moses merely outperformed, or inflated into evidence that occult power is a match for God’s. Scripture allows neither.

expand to see more

The rationalizing reading makes the Egyptian magicians illusionists and the plagues a contest of technique. The text will not support it: they turned rods into serpents and water into blood, and the narrative reports it without qualification, adding only that Aaron’s rod swallowed theirs. Paul names two of them by tradition — as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth (2 Timothy 3:8) — and treats them as a type of real opposition rather than of fraud. Scripture’s consistent testimony is that occult power exists, that it is forbidden (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), and that it is genuinely dangerous. Simon in Samaria bewitched the people and had a following before he ever heard the gospel (Acts 8:9).

The opposite error inflates that admission into dualism, as though two comparable powers were contending. Exodus 8:18 settles it in five words: but they could not. The magicians who had matched two plagues could not produce lice, and they said so to Pharaoh’s face — This is the finger of God. Two plagues later they could not stand in Moses’ presence because they were covered in boils. The limit is not a close-run thing. Daniel makes the same point in Babylon by a different route: the magicians could not tell the king his dream, and Daniel says plainly that the secret is not revealed for any wisdom he has more than any living, but there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets (Daniel 2:28).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew chartom denotes a sacred scribe or engraver — an official skilled in the priestly writings — and is the word used in both the Egyptian and Babylonian courts; the Greek in Acts is mageuo, to practise magic.

expand to see more

Hebrew chartom (H2748) — a sacred scribe, diviner, magician; the court office in Egypt (Genesis 41:24; Exodus 7:11) and Babylon (Daniel 1:20).

Hebrew lahat and lat — secret arts, enchantments; they also did in like manner with their enchantments (Exodus 7:11).

Hebrew 'etsba' 'elohim — the finger of God; the magicians’ own confession (Exodus 8:19), and the phrase our Lord uses of casting out devils (Luke 11:20).

Greek magos (G3097) — a magus; used both of Simon and Elymas as sorcerers, and of the wise men from the east in Matthew 2.

Greek mageuo (G3096) — to practise magic; Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery (Acts 8:9).

Usage

"They also did in like manner with their enchantments (Exodus 7:11) — the power is real, and the narrative does not deny it."

"The magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not (Exodus 8:18) — the limit, reached at the third plague."

"Ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers (Daniel 1:20) — the same contest run again in Babylon, with the same outcome."
